title: How has the Java interface evolved from Java 7 to Java 17+?
shortTitle: How has the Java interface evolved?
keyPoints: Java 7: only abstract methods and static final constants
Java 8: added default methods (with body) and static methods
Java 9: added private methods for code reuse within default methods
Java 14+: sealed interfaces control which classes can implement
Default methods solved the backward-compatibility problem: add new methods to interfaces without breaking existing implementations

s1_definition.oneliner: Interfaces evolved from abstract-only (Java 7) to supporting default methods (Java 8), static methods (Java 8), private methods (Java 9), and sealed restrictions (Java 17).
s1_definition.profdef:
The evolution:

- **Java 7:** Only abstract methods and `static final` constants. Every method must be implemented by the class.
- **Java 8:** Added `default` methods (with a body) and `static` methods. Enabled interface evolution without breaking existing implementations.
- **Java 9:** Added `private` methods for code reuse within default methods.
- **Java 17:** Added `sealed` interfaces to control which classes can implement them.
s1_definition.analogy: Originally, a bank's service agreement (interface) only listed what services a branch must provide (abstract methods). In Java 8, the agreement started including pre-written standard procedures (default methods) that branches could use as-is or customize. In Java 9, the agreement allowed internal helper procedures (private methods). In Java 17, the agreement could specify exactly which branch types are allowed to sign it (sealed).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Java 7:  interface = abstract methods + constants only
  Java 8:  + default methods (body) + static methods
  Java 9:  + private methods (code reuse in defaults)
  Java 17: + sealed (control who implements)

  default method solves:
    interface has 100 implementations
    → add new method with default body
    → all 100 implementations get it free, no changes needed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Interfaces evolved from abstract-method-only contracts (Java 7) to rich constructs with default methods, static methods, private methods, and sealed restrictions. Default methods solved backward compatibility: you can add new methods to an interface without breaking existing implementations. Private methods enable code reuse within default methods. Sealed interfaces control exactly which classes can implement them.

One sentence to remember: Java 8 added default and static methods, Java 9 added private methods, Java 17 added sealed – interfaces are now much more than just abstract method declarations.
